questions.solution:
Sperm are produced in the **seminiferous tubules** of the testis, from spermatogonia at the wall inward.

Two supporting cell types matter: **Sertoli cells** inside the tubules nourish the developing sperm, while **Leydig cells** in the tissue between the tubules secrete **testosterone**.

The **epididymis** stores and matures sperm rather than producing them, and the prostate contributes fluid to the semen.

questions.q: Ovulation in a typical 28-day human menstrual cycle occurs around day:
questions.solution:
Ovulation occurs around **day 14**, triggered by a sharp **surge in luteinising hormone (LH)**.

The cycle runs: menstrual phase (days 1 to 5), follicular phase (6 to 13), **ovulation** (14), and luteal phase (15 to 28).

The LH surge is the immediate cause, and it is itself triggered by the high oestrogen produced by the maturing follicle — one of the few examples of **positive** feedback in human physiology.

questions.q: Fertilisation in humans normally occurs in the:
options: Ampullary region of the fallopian tube
questions.solution:
Fertilisation takes place in the **ampullary-isthmic junction** of the fallopian tube, not the uterus.

Both the sperm and the ovum must reach that point at the same time, which is why fertilisation is far from guaranteed after any single act of intercourse.

The zygote then travels down to the uterus, dividing as it goes, and implants as a **blastocyst** about 6 to 7 days later. An embryo implanting in the tube instead is an **ectopic** pregnancy.

After ovulation the ruptured follicle becomes the **corpus luteum**, which secretes large amounts of **progesterone**.

Progesterone maintains the **endometrium**, preparing it for implantation.

If fertilisation does not occur the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, and the endometrium breaks down — which **is** menstruation. If it does occur, **hCG** from the embryo keeps the corpus luteum alive, and it is hCG that a pregnancy test detects.

questions.q: The structure that implants in the uterine wall is the:
questions.solution:
The **blastocyst** implants, about 6 to 7 days after fertilisation.

The sequence is zygote → 2, 4, 8, 16 cells → **morula** (a solid ball) → **blastocyst** (a hollow ball).

The blastocyst has two parts: the **trophoblast**, an outer layer which attaches to the endometrium and later forms the placenta, and the **inner cell mass**, which becomes the embryo itself.

options: A structure for exchange and also an endocrine gland
questions.solution:
The placenta does two quite different jobs.

**Exchange**: oxygen and nutrients pass from mother to foetus, and carbon dioxide and wastes the other way. Maternal and foetal blood come close but **never mix**.

**Endocrine**: it secretes **hCG**, **hPL**, oestrogen, progesterone and relaxin. This is why the corpus luteum is no longer needed after the first trimester — the placenta has taken over its hormonal role.

questions.q: Which contraceptive method also protects against sexually transmitted infections?
questions.solution:
**Condoms** are the only method listed that acts as a **physical barrier** to the exchange of body fluids, so they protect against STIs including HIV as well as preventing pregnancy.

Pills, IUDs and surgical sterilisation prevent conception but offer **no protection whatever** against infection.

That dual protection is why condoms are promoted even alongside other methods.

questions.q: IVF followed by transfer of an embryo of more than 8 blastomeres into the uterus is called:
questions.solution:
**IUT — intrauterine transfer** — is used for an embryo of **more than 8 blastomeres**, transferred into the **uterus**.

**ZIFT** (zygote intrafallopian transfer) places an embryo of up to 8 blastomeres into the **fallopian tube**.

The logic is developmental: an early embryo is transferred to where it would naturally be at that stage, and a later one to where it would have reached by then.

**GIFT** transfers an ovum rather than an embryo, and **ICSI** injects a single sperm directly into an ovum.

questions.q: Amniocentesis is misused in India for:
questions.solution:
Amniocentesis is a legitimate diagnostic test, sampling amniotic fluid to detect chromosomal abnormalities and metabolic disorders before birth.

Its **misuse** is for sex determination followed by the abortion of female foetuses. This is why **sex determination using it is legally banned in India**, under the PCPNDT Act.

It is a clear case of a beneficial technique needing legal restriction because of how it came to be used — the test itself is unchanged, only its permitted purpose.

questions.q: How many functional sperm are produced from one primary spermatocyte?
questions.solution:
One primary spermatocyte undergoes meiosis I to give 2 secondary spermatocytes, and meiosis II to give $\mathbf{4}$ spermatids, all of which mature into functional sperm.

Contrast **oogenesis**, where one primary oocyte gives just **one** ovum plus three polar bodies that degenerate — the cytoplasm is kept in a single cell rather than shared out, because the ovum must provision the early embryo.

questions.q: How many ova are produced from one primary oocyte?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{1}$ ovum, together with **three polar bodies** that degenerate.

The divisions are deliberately **unequal**: nearly all the cytoplasm goes to the one surviving cell. Sharing it four ways would leave each with too little to support an embryo before implantation.

questions.q: What is the duration, in days, of a typical human menstrual cycle?
questions.solution:
About $\mathbf{28}$ days, though 21 to 35 is within the normal range.

The **luteal** phase after ovulation is the consistent part at about 14 days; most of the variation between women lies in the **follicular** phase before it.

questions.q: What is the normal gestation period in humans, in months?
questions.solution:
About $\mathbf{9}$ months, conventionally 280 days counted from the last menstrual period.

By the end of the first trimester most major organ systems are formed, which is why that period is the most vulnerable to teratogens.

questions.q: How many days after fertilisation does implantation typically occur?
questions.solution:
About $\mathbf{7}$ days, usually quoted as 6 to 7.

The embryo spends that time travelling down the fallopian tube and dividing, reaching the uterus as a blastocyst. It does not implant earlier because only the blastocyst's trophoblast can attach to the endometrium.

questions.q: Describe the hormonal control of the human menstrual cycle through its four phases. Explain what happens differently if fertilisation occurs, and why the fall in progesterone is the immediate cause of menstruation.
questions.solution:
**The hormones involved.** Four matter: **FSH** and **LH** from the anterior pituitary, and **oestrogen** and **progesterone** from the ovary.

**1. Menstrual phase, days 1 to 5.**

Oestrogen and progesterone are both at their lowest. Without progesterone to maintain it, the **endometrium breaks down** and is shed with blood — this is menstruation.

The low hormone levels **release the pituitary from inhibition**, so FSH begins to rise, starting the next cycle.

**2. Follicular (proliferative) phase, days 6 to 13.**

**FSH** stimulates several ovarian follicles, one of which becomes dominant while the rest degenerate.

The growing follicle secretes increasing **oestrogen**, which causes the endometrium to **proliferate** and thicken.

**3. Ovulation, around day 14.**

Here the feedback **reverses**, which is the interesting part. Through most of the cycle oestrogen **inhibits** LH by negative feedback. But once oestrogen passes a threshold and stays high, it begins to **stimulate** LH instead — a switch to **positive** feedback, one of very few in human physiology.

The result is a sharp **LH surge**, which ruptures the follicle and releases the ovum.

**4. Luteal (secretory) phase, days 15 to 28.**

Under LH, the ruptured follicle becomes the **corpus luteum**, secreting large amounts of **progesterone**.

Progesterone **maintains and further prepares** the endometrium, making it thick, well supplied with blood and secretory — ready to receive an embryo. It also suppresses FSH and LH, which prevents another follicle maturing.

**If fertilisation does NOT occur.**

The corpus luteum has a fixed lifespan of about 10 to 12 days and then **degenerates** into the corpus albicans.

Progesterone therefore **falls sharply**. The endometrium, whose blood supply depends entirely on it, can no longer be maintained: the spiral arteries constrict, the tissue becomes ischaemic and breaks down, and it is shed as menstruation.

**This is why the fall in progesterone is the immediate cause.** Menstruation is not something actively triggered — it is the **withdrawal** of the support that was holding the endometrium in place. The lining is being continuously maintained, and it collapses when that maintenance stops.

The falling progesterone also lifts its inhibition of the pituitary, so FSH rises again and the next cycle begins. The cycle is therefore self-restarting.

**If fertilisation DOES occur.**

The problem the embryo faces is precise: the corpus luteum is about to die on schedule, and if it does, the lining the embryo has just implanted in will be shed with the embryo in it.

The solution is that the implanting **trophoblast** secretes **human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)**, which mimics LH and **rescues the corpus luteum**, keeping it alive and secreting progesterone.

So progesterone never falls, the endometrium is never shed, and **menstruation does not occur** — which is the first sign of pregnancy.

hCG is detectable in urine within days of implantation, and detecting it is exactly how a home pregnancy test works.

By the end of the **first trimester** the **placenta** is producing enough progesterone itself, and the corpus luteum is no longer needed. It regresses, and the pregnancy continues unaffected — the handover having already taken place.
